questions.prompt: What is the only legitimate parent of svchost.exe?
questions.explanation: services.exe is the sole legitimate parent of svchost.exe, and every legitimate instance also carries a -k argument naming its service group.

questions.prompt: Why are orphaned processes like explorer.exe and csrss.exe normal rather than suspicious?
options: They are not normal and always indicate compromise
Their parents (userinit.exe and smss.exe) exit deliberately after doing their jobs, leaving the parent PID pointing at a process that no longer exists
Windows randomly reassigns parent PIDs at boot
Orphaned processes cannot exist in Windows
questions.explanation: userinit.exe and smss.exe both exit by design once their startup work is complete, so tools flagging 'missing parent' will report their children every time on a healthy system.

questions.prompt: Why is a parent PID alone insufficient to establish process lineage?
options: PIDs are reused, so you also need the parent's process creation time to be earlier than the child's
Parent PIDs are only recorded on servers
Parent PIDs change every few seconds
questions.explanation: Because Windows reuses PIDs, a parent PID can point at an unrelated process that started later. Sysmon Event ID 1 records both creation times, which is why it is preferred over 4688 for tree reconstruction.

questions.prompt: Why is any child process of lsass.exe among the strongest indicators in Windows forensics?
options: lsass.exe legitimately spawns many children during logon
lsass.exe never spawns child processes under normal operation, so any child is anomalous
Children of lsass.exe are always signed by Microsoft
lsass.exe only has children on domain controllers
questions.explanation: There is exactly one lsass.exe, parented by wininit.exe, and it has no legitimate children. Any child process is a strong credential-access signal.
